newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: CA chief exec's fate in balance after sale.
newsitem.headline: CA chief exec's fate in balance after sale.

text.p: Media speculation grew on Tuesday that Creditanstalt chief executive Guido Schmidt-Chiari was poised to resign following a takeover by Bank Austria, but insiders quashed expectations of an early announcement.
"There will be no board changes while Brussels is scrutinising the deal and what Schmidt-Chiari decides after that is anybody's guess," a well-placed source said.
"But no responsible member of the executive board would go while the ownership structure remains unclear," he added.
The European Commission is probing whether the government sale of the nation's second-largest bank Creditanstalt to market leader Bank Austria involves public subsidies.
Schmidt-Chiari, Creditanstalt chief executive since 1988 and employee since 1958, mounted a public campaign to prevent what he considered an aggressive takeover.
Austrian business daily Wirtschaftswoche quoted the 64-year-old career banker as saying on Tuesday he expected to take "painful steps" when he had spoken to Bank Austria about its future strategy.
"As yet there has been no contact between the two boards and there will not be any until the deal is given clearance by Brussels," the source said.
Bank Austria, which is effectively controlled by the City of Vienna, succeeded at the weekend in a 17.2 billion schilling bid for the state's 70-percent of Creditanstalt voting shares.

A row over the deal, which removes Creditanstalt from the conservative sphere of influence and places it squarely in the Social Democrat camp, brought Austria's left-right coalition government close to collapse.
Creditanstalt's non-executive supervisory board chief Walter Fremuth tendered his resignation on Monday but Bank Austria swiftly asked him to stay on.
Fremuth said other members of the supervisory board and the executive board had to decide for themselves whether they would follow his lead.
